IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No.4244 of 2026
(@Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.10351 of 2026)
Venugopal Jhawar & Anr.
       ...Appellant (s)
Versus
State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
   ...Respondent (s)
O R D E R
Leave granted. 
2. This is a classic case of how the criminal judicial
system can be abused to further personal vendetta. The
first appellant is a Doctor running an establishment
called Deva Institute of Healthcare and Research Pvt.
Ltd., Varanasi and the second respondent was an employee
of  the  said  institute.  On  allegations  of  misconduct
levelled,  the  second  respondent  is  said  to  have
apologized and later resigned from his job. Later to his
resignation,  he  lodged  a  complaint  before  the
jurisdictional police as per Annexure P1, alleging that
on demonetization, the appellants along with three others
in  the  employment  of  the  hospital  summoned  the
complainant to the first appellant’s chamber and sought
1

--- Page 248 ---
details regarding the bank accounts of every member of
the complainant’s household. The complainant was directed
to make a deposit of Rs.2,50,000/- in the said bank
accounts, which the complainant refused to comply with.
Again, he was summoned to the chamber after two days,
where  the  appellant  along  with  other  three  persons
threatened and abused the complainant for not agreeing to
make  deposit  of  Rs.10,00,000/-  into  the  four  bank
accounts of the various members of his family. Later,
Annexure P2 complaint was filed, again making the very
same allegations but detailing the alleged actions of the
appellants herein.
3. The  Additional  Chief  Judicial  Magistrate-III,
Varanasi recorded the statement of the complainant, his
wife and his daughter and issued summons against all the
six accused. The appellants challenged the same before
the learned Sessions Judge, Varanasi, who remanded the
matter to the learned Magistrate. Again, the ACJM III
passed order dated 22.02.2019 produced as Annexure P8,
which led to the instant proceedings before the High
Court.  The  High  Court  on  the  premise  that  the
inconsistencies noticed and the lack of medical evidence
2

--- Page 249 ---
are matters to be adjudicated in a proper trial, refused
to interfere. 
4. The very allegations have a ring of falsehood and the
second  respondent  obviously  has  not  attempted  to
challenge  his  illegal  termination  on  the  alleged
fabrication  of  a  resignation  letter.  The  second
respondent, who admits to have been an employee of the
first  appellant,  though  issued  with  notice,  has  not
appeared before this Court. The very allegation raised is
that the second respondent and his family members were
threatened, abused and assaulted for reason of refusing
to deposit amounts in their personal bank accounts, when
demonetization  was  announced.  The  deposit  of  amounts
after  announcement  of  demonetization  definitely  would
attract scrutiny, and the allegation levelled on the face
of it is false and is only a figment of imagination. Also
considering the fact that the second respondent has not
attempted to challenge his severance from employment,
which is by a resignation letter alleged to have been
obtained from the second respondent through coercion, we
find the complaint itself to be  mala  fide  and a clear
abuse of the process of law. 
3

--- Page 250 ---
5. We find absolutely no reason for ACJM III, Varanasi
to proceed with the complaint No.235/2017 filed before
that Court. We set aside the order passed at Annexure P8
and quash the complaint. No further proceedings shall be
taken in the complaint.
6. The appeal stands allowed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

……..……….……………………. J.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant.
3. The appeal arises from an order dated
26.02.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Judicature at Patna whereby the anticipatory
bail prayer of the appellant was accepted
but a condition was imposed that he shall
pay maintenance at Rs. 10,000/- per month to
the second respondent (the appellant’s wife
herein).
4. The  submission  on  behalf  of  the
1

--- Page 258 ---
appellant is that the second respondent has
filed an application for maintenance and on
the  said  application,  no  order  to  pay
maintenance have yet been passed. In such
circumstances, it has been submitted that
the condition imposed is unjustified as it
precludes the appellant from setting up a
defence against the maintenance application
preferred by the second respondent.
5. We find substance in the aforesaid
submission of the learned counsel for the
appellant.
6. In our view, the impugned condition
ought not to have been imposed in absence of
any order of the competent court granting
such maintenance. As we have been informed
that the application seeking maintenance is
pending, and no orders have yet been passed
directing the appellant to pay maintenance,
we deem it appropriate to set aside the
aforesaid condition.
7. The appeal stands disposed of in the
aforesaid terms.

 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@ Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.  13836/2026)
DHASHRATH SINGH      ...APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN                ….RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the judgment and order dated
19.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Rajasthan at Jodhpur in S.B. Criminal Miscellaneous 2nd
Bail Application No. 5725 of 2025.
The appellant herein has been booked for the crime
registered pursuant to FIR No.3/2023 dated 02.01.2023
lodged with Police Station Rayla, District Bhilwara,
with respect to offences punishable under Sections 8
and  15  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and  Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985.
An  application  seeking  regular bail having been 
1

--- Page 288 ---
rejected by the High Court vide impugned order dated
19.05.2026, the appellant has preferred the instant
appeal.
By order dated 06.08.2026, the following order was 
passed by this Court:
“Issue notice to the respondent, returnable on 
31.08.2026. 
Mr. Saurabh Rajpal, learned counsel accepts  
notice for the respondent-State.”
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and learned counsel appearing for the respondent and
perused the material on record. 
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that
on the fateful day, the appellant was driving the car
which was intercepted containing 70.400 Kg of Poppy
Straw.  The allegations against the appellant are on
the basis that he was in conscious possession of the
said substance whereas the appellant was only the
driver of the car and two other persons/co-accused,
who were in actual possession of the said substance
have  been  granted  bail  by  the  High  Court.  The
appellant has been denied the relief of bail by the
High Court.  Therefore, on the principle of parity,
the appellant  may also be granted the relief of bail
subject to the conditions that may be imposed on the
2

--- Page 289 ---
appellant herein. 
Per contra, learned counsel for  the respondent/State
with reference to her counter affidavit contended that 
there is no merit in this appeal and the High Court was 
justified in declining to grant the relief of bail to the
appellant  herein;  that  there  are  only  seven  more  
witnesses to be examined as twelve out of nineteen  
witnesses have already been examined and hence this  
Court may direct the concerned   Special   Court   to
conclude  the trial expeditiously or otherwise the  
entire trial may be frustrated.  She  therefore,  
submitted that the appeal may be dismissed. 
Considering the facts on record, in our view, the 
case for bail is made out.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and direct as under:
“The  appellant  shall  be  produced  before  the
concerned Trial Court as early as possible and
the  Trial  Court  shall  release  him  on  bail,
subject  to  such  conditions  as  it  may  deem
appropriate to impose to ensure his presence in
the proceedings arising out of FIR/Case No. 3 of
2023 dated 02.01.2023 mentioned above.”
It   is   directed  that the appellant  shall extend 
3

--- Page 290 ---
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation.
The appellant shall not misuse his liberty and shall 
not in any way influence the witnesses or tamper with 
the material on record.
Any  infraction  of  the  conditions  may  entail  
cancellation of bail granted to the appellant.
With the aforesaid directions, the criminal appeal is
allowed.       
 ………………………………………J.
  [B.V. NAGARATHNA]
 ….……………………………………J.
   [R. MAHADEVAN]
 NEW DELHI
    SEPTEMBER 07, 2026

Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the order dated 02.04.2026
passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Indore in
Misc. Criminal Case No. 12281 of 2026. 
This criminal appeal arises out of crime registered
pursuant to FIR No. 433 of 2022 dated 25.12.2022 lodged
with Police  Station –  Susner, District  Agar Malwa
(M.P.), for the offences punishable under Sections 147,
148, 353, 341, 323, 294, 506, 332 and 427 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860, as well as Section 3 of the M.P.
Sampatti Virupan Nivaran Adhiniyam, 1994. Anticipating
arrest in connection with this crime, the appellant
1

--- Page 293 ---
preferred Misc. Criminal Case No. 12281 of 2026 before
the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Indore seeking
anticipatory bail.
By impugned order dated 02.04.2026, the High Court
dismissed the application for anticipatory bail. Hence,
the present appeal. 
By order dated 07.08.2026 this Court while issuing
notice in the instant matter granted interim protection
from arrest to the appellant. 
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and learned counsel appearing for the respondent/State
and perused the material on record. 
Learned  counsel for the appellant submitted that
although the FIR is dated 25.12.2022, the appellant has
neither  been  summoned  nor  notified  to  join  the
investigation for the last nearly four years. However, the
other  co-accused  have  been  granted  regular  bail.  The
appellant herein is a Government servant and he is working
as a  Patwari and he had no role to play in the entire
incident. In the circumstances, this Court had granted
interim protection subject to the appellant co -operating
with the investigation. However, the appellant has not
been summoned even till date. Hence, the interim order
granted by this Court may be made absolute. 
2

--- Page 294 ---
Per  contra,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent/State submitted that there is no merit in
this appeal and the same may be dismissed. 
Considering the circumstances on record, in our
view, the appellant is entitled to the relief of
anticipatory bail.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and set aside
the order passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh
at Indore dated 02.04.2026. We direct that in the
event  of  arrest  of  the  appellant,  the  Arresting
Officer shall release the appellant on bail, subject
to furnishing cash security in the sum of Rs.25,000/-
(Rupees  Twenty-Five  Thousand  only)  with  two  like
sureties.
It is directed that the appellant shall extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation.
In case, the appellant is directed to appear
before the Investigating Officer on any particular
date, he shall comply with the said direction.
 The appellant shall not misuse his liberty and
shall not in any way influence the witnesses or tamper
with the material on record.
3

--- Page 295 ---

This appeal challenges the judgment and order
dated  01.07.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Judicature at Patna in Criminal Miscellaneous No.
7332/2026.
The appellant has been facing trial in connection
with crime registered pursuant to FIR No. 356/2024
dated 23.10.2024 registered with P.S. Teghra, District
Begusarai in respect of offences punishable under
Sections 08 and 20(b)(ii)(c) of the Narcotic Drugs and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (“NDPS Act”).
An application seeking regular bail having been
rejected by the High Court vide impugned order dated
01.07.2026, the appellant is before us by way of this
appeal.

--- Page 303 ---
2
This Court vide its order dated 14.08.2026 passed
the following order:
“Issue notice, returnable on 07.09.2026. 
Mr. Samir Ali Khan, learned Advocate-on-
Record  has  put  in  appearance  on  behalf  of
respondent-State of Bihar and accepts notice.
Service on respondent is, accordingly, waived. 
Let learned counsel for the respondent-
State place on record the FSL report along with
the counter affidavit within three weeks.”
Heard  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  in
support of the appeal and learned counsel for the
State and perused the material on record. 
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that
the appellant has been in jail since 24.10.2024 except
for a short period when he was granted interim bail
owing to the death of his father;  the appellant was
only seeking a lift in the swift Dzire car that was
apprehended on the fateful day; the driver of the
vehicle has been granted bail; the co-passenger has
also  been  granted  the  relief  of  bail.  In  the
circumstances,  the  incarceration  of  the  appellant
herein may not be just and proper. The High Court was
not right in declining to grant the relief of bail to
the appellant herein. In the circumstances, the said
order may be set aside and subject to the terms and

--- Page 304 ---
3
conditions that may be imposed by this Court, the
relief of bail may be granted to the appellant herein
on the principle of parity.
Per contra, learned standing counsel for the
respondent-State  with  reference  to  the  counter
affidavit contended that the there are only four out
of nine witnesses to be examined and therefore a
direction may be issued to the Special Court to
conclude the trial expeditiously or otherwise the
trial itself may be jeopardized if the relief of bail
is granted to the appellant herein. He submitted that
there is no merit in this appeal and the same may be
dismissed.
 Considering the facts on record, in our view, the
case for bail is made out.
    We, therefore, allow this appeal and direct as
under:
“The appellant shall be produced before the
concerned Trial Court as early as possible and
the Trial Court shall release him on bail,
subject to such conditions as it may deem

in the proceedings arising out of FIR bearing
No. 356/2024 mentioned above.”

(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant is an accused in Special (NDPS Act) Case
No.175 of 2024, arising out of DRI Unit Case No.02/2024-
25, registered under Sections 20(b)(ii)(C)/25/29 of the
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for
short, ‘NDPS Act’).

owner of the vehicle which was travelling from Guwahati
1

--- Page 308 ---
(Assam) to Daudnagar (Bihar). On interception and search,
65.60 kgs of ganja was recovered from the said vehicle.
6. Appellant was arrested on 16.08.2024 and since then,
he has been in custody.
7. This Court had issued notice vide the order dated
12.06.2026, pursuant to which respondent-Union of India
has filed counter-affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that though
he had purchased the vehicle, the same has not yet been
transferred in his name. The vehicle was driven by one
person who had an accomplice with him. Those two were

statement  that  appellant  came  to  be  arrested.  Since

the trial instead of enlarging the appellant on bail.

having regard to the period of incarceration undergone by
the appellant and the fact that trial may take some more
time to reach its conclusion, we are of the view that a
case for grant of bail is made out.

--- Page 309 ---

maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he shall
be released on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
deemed appropriate. Needless to say, appellant shall co-

registered at Police Station- Kotla Mubarakpur, New Delhi
under  Sections  20/25  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS Act’).

1

--- Page 313 ---
apprehended on 17.01.2025 from the 2 nd floor of a premises
at Kotla Mubarakpur, New Delhi. In the course of search of

forensic examination turned out to be 1.516 kgs of charas.
6. Pursuant  thereto,  appellant  was  arrested  on
17.01.2025 and since then, he is in custody.

8. Since  a  submission  was  made  on  behalf  of  the

to  the  appellant,  we  called  upon  the  learned  Addl.

arrest strikes at the very root of the arrest, rendering
the same illegal. An illegal arrest cannot be continued.

are yet to be examined.

SONU @MONU @ASHUTOSH NISHAD                        Appellant(s)

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  learned  counsel  for  the
parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order
dated 04.12.2025 passed by the High Court of
Chhattisgarh  at  Bilaspur  rejecting  the
regular bail prayer of the appellant in
connection  with  Crime  No.  360/2025,
registered at P.S. Simga, District Baloda-
Bazar-Bhatapara (C.G.).
4. The  submission  on  behalf  of  the
appellant is that he was not named in the
First Information Report. Later, as many as
1

--- Page 333 ---
16 persons were implicated out of those 16,
2 were juvenile. It has been submitted that
co-accused  Sanju  Banjare,  who  has  been
attributed identical role, has been granted
bail  by  this  Court  vide order  dated
16.03.2026  passed  in  Criminal  Appeal
No. ...of 2026 @ SLP (Crl) No.1038/2026.
5. The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail
on the ground that appellant had criminal
antecedents.
6. In respect thereof, the appellant has
provided a chart to disclose that in 5 out
of 6 cases, he has been acquitted and the
other case which is pending relates to minor
offence.
7. The  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State submits that having regard
to the criminal antecedents, the case of the
appellant is distinguishable from the one
who has been granted bail.
8. We have considered the submissions.
Having regard to the nature of allegations
2

--- Page 334 ---
as  also  that  other  co-accused  has  been
granted bail, we are of the view that the
appellant, who has been in jail for a period
exceeding  one  year,  is  entitled  to  be
released on bail pending trial. 
9. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the
regular bail prayer of the appellant is set
aside.
10. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the
trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

PRIYANKA           ...PETITIONER

O R D E R
1. The present Transfer Petition has been filed for transfer of the
divorce proceedings initiated by the respondent-Husband in Case
No.2412 of 2025, titled as “Manish v. Priyanka & Anr.” from the Court
of Principal Judge, Family Court, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh to the Court
of Principal Judge, Family Court, Pune, Maharashtra.
2. This Court having noticed the possibility of arriving at a
settlement between the parties being there, referred the dispute to
the Supreme Court Mediation Centre vide  order dated 22.05.2026.
Accordingly, the parties appeared before the Mediation Centre and
after due deliberations, they have arrived at a settlement. The Report
forwarded by the Mediation Centre would disclose that the parties
have entered into a Settlement Agreement dated 15.07.2026.
3. Both the parties are present virtually and admit the execution
of the Settlement Agreement.  They have also reiterated the contents
of the Settlement Agreement and stated that said Settlement
Agreement has been entered into voluntarily without any force, threat
1

--- Page 338 ---
or coercion and only after having understood the contents of the
same, they have affixed their signatures voluntarily.  The respective
learned advocates representing the parties and who are present
before the Court, in token of having identified the parties, have also
affixed their signatures to the Settlement Agreement.
4. Along with the Settlement Agreement, a joint application under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India being I.A. No. 268012 of 2026
for grant of a decree of divorce by mutual consent is also filed
whereunder, the parties seek for dissolution of marriage solemnized
between them on 12.12.2021 on the ground that there is no
compatibility and on account of irreconcilable differences of opinion
having arisen between them and they are unable to cohabit and as
such, they have sought for dissolution of marriage.
5. This Court having interacted with the parties who were present
virtually and being satisfied that both the parties are fully conversant
with the consequences of the settlement and also being satisfied that
there is no possibility of reunion between them, as such, the prayer
sought for in the application deserves to be granted and the marriage
solemnized between the parties on 12.12.2021, stands dissolved. 
6. Registry to draw a decree of divorce in terms of the settlement
referred to in paragraphs 5 to 9 of the Settlement Agreement dated
15.07.2026.
7. Accordingly, the Transfer Petition stands disposed of in the
above terms.

--- Page 339 ---

9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.12470 of 2026
(@Special Leave Petition (C) No.32974 of 2025)
Pramod Kumar Rao @ Munna Singh
       ...Appellant
Versus
Legal Head Sahara India
Commercial Corporation Ltd.
Office Sahara India & Ors.
     ...Respondents
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. A civil suit was filed on 17.02.2020 by the appellant herein, in
which the respondent was the defendant. The respondent despite
appearance before court, failed to file written statement. Much later
on 15.07.2024, an application was filed under Order VII Rule 11 of
the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) read with Section 8 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (the Act) projecting the
arbitration clause in the agreement between the parties.

--- Page 342 ---
2
3. The Court of the Civil Judge (Senior Division) allowed the
application filed by the defendant and rejected the plaint of the
appellant. The first appeal before the High Court was rejected, which
is impugned in the present petition.
4. It is very evident from Annexure P6, a response to a query
under the Right to Information Act, 2005, that the suit was filed as
early as in 2020 as Suit No.120 of 2020. Summons was issued with
next date of hearing as on 17.04.2021. The application filed by the
respondent pointing out the arbitration clause as produced at
Annexure P2 does not even speak of the specific arbitration clause as
available in the agreement between the parties. Admittedly, the
defendant, despite appearance, did not file a written statement and
the plea of arbitration was raised after four years.
5. We find absolutely no reason to uphold the order of the Civil
Court as affirmed by the High Court, especially considering the delay
in raising a plea of arbitration. In fact, the prayer in the suit is for

--- Page 343 ---
3
injunction from eviction and not declaration or even handing over of
the flat, in which event the original agreement, with respect to
allotment of flat on the application of purchase, has absolutely no
relevance. The impugned order of the High Court and that of the Civil
Court produced at Annexure P5 are set aside. The Civil Judge (Senior
Division), Gorakhpur shall proceed with Suit No.120 of 2020 from the
stage at which it stood rejected as per Annexure P5.
6. The appeal stands allowed. 
7. We make it clear that we have not stated anything on the
merits of the case, which shall be decided on the adjudication as
carried out by the Civil Court based on valid evidence led.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

of  the  offences  punishable  under  Sections  316(2),

preferred an application before the High Court in terms
of  Section  482  of  the  Bharatiya  Nagarik  Suraksha
Sanhita, 2023 [in short, “BNSS”]
1

--- Page 358 ---
Said application for anticipatory bail has been
rejected by the High Court vide the impugned order
dated  15.04.2026  Hence,  instant  appeal  has  been
preferred.
By order dated 26.05.2026, while issuing notice,
this Court granted interim protection in favour of the
appellant.
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and learned counsel appearing for the respondent/State
and perused the material on record. 
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the
appellant has been co-operating with the investigation.
Hence, the interim order granted by this Court may be made
absolute  and  the  relief  of  anticipatory  bail  may  be
granted to the appellant herein subject to the terms and
condition that may be imposed on the appellant herein. 
Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent/State
submitted that no doubt the appellant has been co-
operating with the investigation and contended that
appropriate orders may be made in the matter. 
Taking note of the submissions advanced by the
parties, we find that in the facts and circumstances
of this case, interim order has to be made absolute.
2

--- Page 359 ---
 
We, therefore, allow this appeal and set aside the 
order passed by the High Court dated 15.04.2026. We  
direct that in the event of arrest of the appellant, 
the Arresting Officer shall release the appellant on bail

Rs.25,000/- (Rupees Twenty-Five Thousand only) with two 
like sureties.
It is directed that the appellant shall extend  
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation. The 
appellant shall not misuse his liberty and shall not in 
any way influence the witnesses or tamper with the  
material on record.
With the aforesaid directions, the criminal appeal 
is allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
EXTRAORDINARY APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
Special Leave Petition (Crl) No…….…….of 2026 
(@ Diary No.20597 of 2026) 
 
 
STATE OF U.P.                                     
 ….PETITIONER 
VERSUS 
SUBHASH CHANDRA & ORS.                            
….RESPONDENT(S) 
O R D E R 
 
Delay condoned.  
2. The State has filed the above Special Leave Petition 
aggrieved by the various directions issued by a learned Single 
Judge in Paragraph 33 of the impugned judgment and order dated 
12.05.2025.  
3. The application under Section 482 of Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1973 (CrPC), was made by the applicants, who were 
summoned by the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate (ACJM) on 
a protest petition, when the investigation pursuant to an FIR, 
registered on the directions of the ACJM was completed and a 
closure report was filed before Court.   
4. While the matter was in seisin of the High Court, the High 
Court thought it fit to streamline criminal investigations, 
especially finding that the Court’s board is choked with many 

--- Page 366 ---
Page 2 of 4 
 
 
such petitions under Section 482 CrPC. Finding the investigation 
procedures to be old and outdated and also stressing upon the 
significance of training programmes, the Director General of 
Police (Training) was summoned, who appeared through video 
conferencing. On the directions of the Court, the DGP (Training) 
prepared a comprehensive checklist for each category of similar 
offences to assist police officers. The Additional DGP (Crime) and 
the DGP (Prosecution) were also summoned and directions 
issued, based on which, it was observed so in Paragraph 32 which 
is extracted hereinbelow: -  
“32.Arising out of the aforesaid deliberations, and 
after considering the submissions advanced by the 
learned Additional Advocate General, as well as upon 
examining the checklist prepared by the office of the 
Director General of Police (Prosecution), along  with 
the numerous circulars and training course materials 
submitted by the Director General of Police (Training) 
contained in five volumes totalling  1,282 pages, the 
Directorate of Prosecution has broadly categorized the 
offences into 41 chapters and formulated a separate 
checklist for each chapter. The compiled checklists 
collectively span a total of 390 pages.” 
 
5. The learned Single Judge then further issued directions as 
per Paragraph 33, which the State is aggrieved with; according to 
us justifiably so. 

--- Page 367 ---
Page 3 of 4 
 
 
6. The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was in place and as 
of now, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 has 
reckoned new modes of investigation and brought in methods 
and measures to have procedures prescribed for collection of 
digital records as evidence and updated the forensic measures. 
7. We are of the opinion that when such measures are in 
place delineating the procedure to be adopted, the Constitutional 
Courts should desist from taking up the task of administering or 
even instructing the State as to how the criminal justice 
administration system has to function. When pitfalls are brought 
to their notice, the Courts could step in, but not in the nature of 
omnibus directions, as has been done by the learned Single 
Judge. 
8. We cannot but notice that the summoning order issued by 
the ACJM was quashed, validating the closure report by the Police 
and no cause arose to call up the police or delineate the 
procedure to carry out a criminal investigation. We see from the 
extracted paragraph above that a checklist was made operative 
by the Director General of Police; which could be followed. 
However, we are unable to concur with the omnibus directions 
issued under Paragraph 33 and, hence, we delete the same. 

--- Page 368 ---
Page 4 of 4 
 
 
9. The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of with the 
above directions. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

                     (J. B. PARDIWALA) 
 
 
....……….……………………. J.

days from the date of release.

appellant, we modify the sentence to the period already undergone
by the appellant. Appellant shall be released forthwith from
custody.

Authority, Mangaluru to ensure that immediate family members of the

Criminal Procedure, 1973 (‘CrPC’).

Only) that would be deposited by the appellant shall be released to

identification.

DANISHKHAN @ D.K. @
DOLLAR MOHSINKHAN PATHAN      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF GUJARAT     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Gujarat.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
17.02.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Gujarat  at
Ahmedabad  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’  hereinafter),
rejecting the regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  C.R.  No.III-01/2025
registered at Police Station- A.T.S., Ahmedabad City,
Gujarat under Sections 8(c), 22(c) and 29 of the Narcotic
Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short,
‘NDPS Act’).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that contraband
in the nature of Mephedrone weighing about 55 grams was
recovered  from  Accused  No.1.  As  per  the  disclosure
statement  of  Accused  No.1,  the  said  contraband  was
1

--- Page 382 ---
procured at the behest of the appellant.
6. Appellant was arrested on 24.07.2025 and since then,
he has been in custody.
7. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
03.08.2026, pursuant to which respondent-State of Gujarat
has filed counter-affidavit.
8. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that
appellant has been apprehended purely on the basis of
suspicion.  No  contraband  was  recovered  from  his
possession,  conscious  or  otherwise.  According  to  the
disclosure statement of Accused No.1, the contraband was
procured at the instance of a second accused and it is the
allegation  that  the  ultimate  destination  was  the
appellant. Appellant is in custody since 24.07.2025. The
trial has not yet commenced. Therefore, appellant may be
enlarged on bail.
9. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Gujarat,
on the other hand, has referred to the counter affidavit
filed on behalf of the respondent-State of Gujarat and
submits that appellant has 03 other criminal antecedents,
all connected with NDPS offences. She submits that charge-
sheet has been filed and the matter is now at the stage of
framing of charges.
10. Responding to the above submissions, learned counsel
for the appellant submits that in all the 03 instances of
antecedents, appellant is on bail. In fact, on the date he
was enlarged on bail in the 3 rd instance, he was roped in
2

--- Page 383 ---
the present case.
11. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that a case for
grant of bail is made out.
12. Having regard to the above, the impugned order dated
17.02.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  is  set  aside.
Consequently,  we  direct  that  the  appellant  shall  be
produced before the jurisdictional Special Court within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he shall
be released on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
deemed appropriate. Since there are antecedents of the
appellant, we direct that the appellant shall appear
before the concerned police station on the 01 st Monday of
every  month  at  11:00  AM  till  such  time  the  trial
commences, whereafter he shall co-operate with the trial.
13. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
@ SLP (CRL.) @ DIARY NO.49992/2026
   KUNU PUJHARI                                       APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
   STATE OF ODISHA                                   RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant as
well as learned counsel for the Respondent – State of
Odisha.
4. Appellant has been convicted by the Court of learned
Additional Sessions Judge, Dharamgarh in the State of
Odisha for committing offence under Sections 302/34 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and sentenced to undergo
imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs.5,000/-
(Rupees Five Thousand only) with a default stipulation vide
the judgment and order dated 31.01.2019.
5. Appellant being the convict, is in jail.
6. From jail, he preferred Criminal Appeal No.929 of
2023  before  the  High  Court  of  Orissa  at  Cuttack
1

--- Page 398 ---
(hereinafter referred to as ‘ the High Court’) assailing
his conviction and sentence. However, there was delay of
1235 days in preferring the appeal. By the impugned order
dated 04.09.2023, the High Court declined to condone the
delay and subsequently, dismissed the Criminal Appeal of
the appellant.
7. In  the  meanwhile,  appellant  has  undergone
approximately ten years of actual incarceration.
8. The fact that appellant is in jail, itself was
sufficient for the High Court to have taken a pragmatic
view of the matter while considering condonation of delay.
After all, it is a statutory right of a convict to file an
appeal under Section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973 (CrPC) against his conviction and sentence. Instead of
taking a pragmatic view of the matter, the High Court
simply dismissed the application for condonation of delay
by observing that appellant sat over the matter for a long
time and did not avail the opportunities available in the
jail.
9. We do not approve of the view taken by the High
Court. Such a view goes against the very concept of justice
itself, more particularly, the principle of access to
justice.
2

--- Page 399 ---

O R D E R
1. Heard counsel for both the parties.
2. The Petitioner has filed the above Transfer Petitions seeking
transfer of two different proceedings one pending before the
Court of Judicial Magistrate Sr. No.9, Jaipur Metropolitan-II,
Jaipur, Rajasthan, and the other case pending before the Court
of the Additional Senior Civil Judge and Additional Chief
Judicial Magistrate Sr. No.2, Jaipur Metropolitan-II, Jaipur,
Rajasthan, to the District Court at Pune, Maharashtra.
3. The Petitioner is the husband of Respondent.  The Petitioner
is a Dentist practicing in Pune and the Respondent is a
permanent resident of Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada, where she
has been residing since 2020.  Earlier, she had filed two
petitions  before  the  Family  Judge,  Sr.  No.4,  Jaipur
Metropolitan,  Jaipur,  Rajasthan,  for  divorce  and  for
maintenance which were both transferred to the District Judge,
Pune, Maharashtra by an order of this Hon’ble Court dated
20.11.2025 in TP(C) No. 1651/2025.  Subsequent to the same,

--- Page 402 ---
the parties had allegedly entered into a settlement which did
not fructify.  Subsequent to that, it is alleged that the
present proceedings under Section 12 of the DV Act and
criminal proceedings under Section 85 and 316(2) of the BNS
were  instituted  before  the  Additional  Chief  Judicial
Magistrate Court in Jaipur by the Respondent against the
Petitioner.
4. From the submission of the parties, it is clear that the
Petitioner  is  an  ordinary  resident  of  Pune,  Maharashtra
whereas the Respondent is the permanent resident of Canada.
It  is  also  a  fact  that  earlier  proceedings  have  been
transferred  to  Pune,  Maharashtra  and  they  are  pending
consideration in the Pune Courts.
5. Having heard the counsel for the parties and on a perusal of
the records we find that the Petitioner had made out a case
for transfer of the aforesaid cases.
6. The apprehension of the Respondent that the expenditure of the
witnesses for travelling from Jaipur to Pune can be met by
passing a direction to the Petitioner to take care of the
same.
7. It is the prayer of the Respondent that the witnesses, if any,
from her side can be permitted to be examined through virtual
mode by the Courts in Pune and if it is not permitted the
expenditure may be borne by the Petitioner.
8. In the result, the Transfer Petitions are allowed, and the
following directions are passed:-
(i) The case No.594/2025 (arising out of FIR No.317/2025

--- Page 403 ---
dated 03.11.2025) presently pending before the Hon’ble
Court of Additional Senior Civil Judge and Additional
Chief Judicial Magistrate, Sr. No.2, Jaipur Metropolitan-
II, Jaipur, Rajasthan, is transferred to the file of
Hon’ble District Court, Pune, Maharashtra.
(ii) Criminal Misc. Case No. 17/2025, presently pending before
the Hon’ble Court of Judicial Magistrate, Sr. No.9,
Jaipur  Metropolitan-II,  Rajasthan,  is  transferred  to
District Judge, Pune, Maharashtra.
(iii) On an Application made by the Respondent, the transferee
court shall permit the Respondent to appear through video
conference on all dates except on the dates on which her
personal presence is absolutely mandatory.
(iv) On an Application made by the Respondent, the transferee
court shall permit the witnesses of the Respondent or the
Petitioner to appear through video conference on all the
dates except when their personal presence is absolutely
mandatory.
(v) Whenever the witnesses of the Respondent are summoned to
appear in-person to the transferee Court in Pune, the
expenditure for the same will be borne by the petitioner.
9. The Transfer Petitions stand allowed in the aforesaid terms.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

appellant is that by now the appellant has
suffered incarceration for a period of about
eight  years.  Besides  the  charge  of  an
offence punishable under the Protection of
Children  from  Sexual  Offences  Act,  2012
1

--- Page 406 ---
(“POCSO Act”) was dropped as the victim was
not a minor. It has also been submitted that
there is no corroboration to the prosecution
case by medical evidence in as much as no
injuries were found on the body of the
victim. 
5. The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail
by  submitting  that  the  prosecutrix  has
supported the prosecution case. 
6. Having  considered  the  rival
submissions and having regard to the fact
that  the  appellant  has  suffered
incarceration of about eight years and the
appeal of the appellant before the High
Court is of the year 2025 and there is no
likelihood of the appeal being heard in near
future, we are of the view that this is a
fit case where the sentence be suspended
pending consideration of his appeal.
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.

the prayer of the appellant for suspension

cost ought not to have been imposed.

waived.

appellant submitted that in the portion where the Court has imposed

unnecessary  embarrassment  for  the  employer,  which  may  cause
problems for him later in his career. Thus, a prayer was made that
the Court may expunge the said reference.
9. Having considered the request, the Court is inclined to allow
the said prayer also.
10. Accordingly, the portion “(who is working as a Manager, Legal
in Godrej)” in paragraph 11 of the impugned order stands expunged.

appearing for the respondent-State.
        SLP (Criminal) No.16624/2024                                                               Page 1 of 3

--- Page 449 ---
2. The  present  Special  Leave  Petition  calls  in
question the correctness of the order dated  12th July,
2019 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras,
Madurai Bench in Criminal Appeal (MD) No.274 of 2017. By
the said order, the  High Court dismissed the Criminal
Appeal and upheld the judgment and order of the Trial
Court dated 17th December, 2015 whereby the petitioner was
convicted under Sections 376 read with 511 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (for short, “the IPC”) and was sentenced
to life imprisonment along with fine of Rs.25,000/-, in
default of payment of fine, to undergo S.I. for one year.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that
the petitioner has been sentenced to life imprisonment,
while the conviction is under Section 376 read with 511
of  the  IPC.  Learned  counsel, drawing  attention to
Section 511 of the IPC, submits that in a case under
Section 511 of the IPC,  which deals with punishment for
attempting  to  commit  an  offence,  punishable  with
imprisonment for life or other imprisonment, the sentence
imposable is a term which may extend to one-half of
imprisonment for life or, as the case may be, one-half of
the  longest  term  of  imprisonment  provided  for  that
offence.
        SLP (Criminal) No.16624/2024                                                               Page 2 of 3

--- Page 450 ---
4. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
submits that imprisonment for life should be understood
as imprisonment for the entire period of life.
5. At this stage, Mr. P.B.Suresh Kumar, learned senior
counsel who is present in Court, draws attention to
Section 57 of the IPC which reads as under:
“57. Fractions of terms of punishment.—
In calculating fractions of terms of punishment,
imprisonment  for  life  shall  be  reck oned  as
equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years.”
6. Applying Section 57 of the IPC, the maximum that
could have been imposed is 10 years.  The petitioner has
already undergone 11 years.
7. We direct that pending disposal of the present
petition, the petitioner shall be enlarged on bail to the
satisfaction of the Trial Court.  
8. We request Mr. P.B.Suresh Kumar, learned senior
counsel to assist the Court as amicus curiae.
9. Let a copy of the paper book be given to the
learned amicus curiae.
10. List the petition for hearing on 9th December, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
EXTRAORDINARY APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
Special Leave to Appeal (C) No(s). 25197 of 2026 
 
 
GOKUL CHAND MANOJ KUMAR AND SONS  
(GM AND SONS) PRIVATE LIMITED & ANR.                                  
 ….PETITIONERS 
VERSUS 
K.A.S. ZAINULABDIN AND CO.                            
….RESPONDENT(S) 
O R D E R 
 
 The short question arising in the above case is whether the 
defendant had satisfactorily explained the delay caused in filing 
the written statement in a Commercial Suit.   
2. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent -
plaintiff, however, pointed out that the written statement was 
filed after the 120 days’ period.  
3. On a reading of the impugned order, we find that the 
summons was received by the defendant on 30.05.2025 and the 
120 days’ period, within which the written statement has to  be 
filed, in a Commercial Suit, with application for condonation of 
delay ends on 27.09.2025. The written statement was affirmed on 
18.09.2025 and on 23.09.2025, the Master’s summons was taken 
out, seeking condonation of delay and acceptance of the written 
statement. Due to the intervening annual vacations, the 

--- Page 461 ---
Page 2 of 3 
 
 
returnable date of the Master’s summons was given as 
28.10.2025. An application was filed on 27.10.2025, seeking 
permission to file the written statement which also was affirmed 
within 120 days. The Court found absolutely no reason to deny 
the prayer; whic h we agree with, in the peculiar facts and 
circumstances of this case.  
4. However, the Court found that the reasons stated for 
condonation of delay was not satisfactory. We have looked at the 
specific paragraphs noticed by the Court, being paragraphs 4, 
6, 7 and 8 of the application filed which is produced as Annexure 
P1 before this Court. We are quite conscious of the fact that the 
satisfaction arrived at insofar as the reasons stated is 
discretionary in nature and normally, a Court sitting in appeal 
would not substitute the discretion, with a reasoning of its own.  
However, we find that the affidavit speaks of having received the 
summons and immediately seeking legal assistance and the 
instructions received to collect documents for preparation of the 
written statement which took considerable time.  
5. In any event, the written statement was finalized on 
18.09.2025 within 120 days of the receipt of the summons. We are 
of the opinion that the Court ought to have found the reasons to 
be satisfactory, since otherwise, the defendant would be unable 

--- Page 462 ---
Page 3 of 3 
 
 
to put -forth his contentions before the Court. Ends of justice 
requires the delay to be condoned on the explanation offered. 
We, hence, set aside the order to that extent, finding the reasons 
stated for delay to be satisfactory.   
6. We direct the written statement to be accepted, and the 
case shall be proceeded with, in accordance with law.   
7. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition 
stands disposed of.   
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.    
 
 
.......…….……………………. J. 
                     (J. B. PARDIWALA) 
 
 
....……….……………………. J. 
                             (K. VINOD CHANDRAN) 
 
NEW DELHI;

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioners (home buyers) have invoked the writ
jurisdiction  of  this  Court  under  Article  32  of  the
Constitution seeking the following reliefs:-
“(a) Declare that the Petitioners and all similarly
situated allottees of the Hi-Tech Township at Lucknow
developed under the name and style of "Sushant Golf
City" have a fundamental right under Article 21 of the
Constitution of India to secure, timely and habitable
possession  of  the  units  allotted  to  them;
(b) Issue a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate
writ, order or direction directing Respondent No. 4 to
take over and complete the development of the Hi-Tech
Township at Lucknow and to hand over possession of the
completed units to the allottees thereof in a time-bound
manner;

--- Page 473 ---
(c) Direct Respondent No. 4 to place before this Hon'ble
Court a comprehensive Completion Proposal and Terms of
Reference setting out, at the least:
(i) the project-wise scope of the takeover and
the  present  physical,  legal  and  regulatory
status  of  each  constituent  project  of  the
Township;
(ii)  a  phased  construction  programme  with
completion timelines for each project;
(iii) the sources and application of funds,
including the monetisation of the 25% of total
saleable land retained and mortgaged in favour
of  Respondent  No.  4,  the  receivables  from
allottees  falling  due  upon  achievement  of
milestones, and the unsold inventory of the
Township;
(iv) the treatment of existing allottees, who
shall not be subjected to any escalation of cost
save  as  payable  under  their  subsisting
agreements, and the mechanism for handover of
possession  and  execution  of  registered
conveyances in their favour;
(v)  the  statutory  approvals,  sanctions  and
renewals required and the authorities from whom
they are to be obtained; and
(vi)  the  treatment  of  receipts,  costs  and
surplus, and of the claims of creditors and land
authorities;
(d)  Constitute  a  monitoring  mechanism  for  the
implementation  of  the  completion  proposal,  if  any,
submitted by Respondent No. 6;
(e) Direct a court-monitored forensic audit, by an
independent firm of forensic auditors to be appointed by
this  Hon'ble  Court  and  into  the  collection  and
utilisation of all sums received from the allottees of
the Hi-Tech Township at Lucknow;
(f) Direct Respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 and all other
statutory authorities whose sanction, approval, renewal
or no-objection is required for the completion of the
Township to consider and communicate their decisions
upon the applications made in that behalf within thirty
days of the making thereof;
(g) Pass such other and further order or orders as this
Hon'ble Court may deem just, fit and proper in the facts
and circumstances of the case and in the interests of
justice.”

--- Page 474 ---
2. Having heard Mr. K. Parameshwar, the learned senior
counsel appearing for the petitioners and having looked
into the reliefs prayed for, we are of the view that the
petitioners should go before the territorial High Court
under Article 226 of the Constitution seeking the reliefs
as prayed for in the present petition.
3. If any such Writ Petition is preferred, the High Court
shall look into the same expeditiously, considering the
plight and difficulties of the home buyers.
4. In view of the aforesaid, the Writ Petition stands
disposed of.
5. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.

1. The  petitioner  seeks  enlargement  on  bail  in  FIR

Rajnandgaon, Chhattisgarh. After investigation, charge-sheet

Act, 2002 and Sections 111, 338, 336(3), and 340(2) of
1

--- Page 494 ---
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
2. The allegations are that a bulk quantity comprising 3888
litres of illicit liquor was recovered from a raid conducted
on 29.03.2025 at the farmhouse of the petitioner’s co-accused
Rohit Netam alias Sonu. Large-scale empty bottles, holograms,
and  sealing  material  were  also  recovered  at  the  spot,
indicating that the locally manufactured liquor was being sold
with fake packaging by a syndicate. The petitioner’s name
emerged  during  the  course  of  investigation,  and  he  was
consequently arrested on 05.04.2025. 
3. It seems that the petitioner is a habitual offender, as
three more such-like cases are registered against him.
4. However,  the  fact  remains  that  the  petitioner  has
remained  custody  for  over  1  year  and  5  months.  The
investigation is also complete, given that the final report
has been filed. There are 25 witnesses likely to be examined,
and hence, conclusion of trial will take some time.
5. Taking into consideration the totality of circumstances,
but without expressing any opinion on merits, the prayer for
bail is allowed. The petitioner is directed to be released on
bail subject to his furnishing bail bonds to the satisfaction
of the Trial Court.
6. The petitioner shall weekly report to the jurisdictional
police station for certification of his good conduct while on
bail. In case he is found to have indulged in similar offences
2

--- Page 495 ---
again,  the  instant  order  shall  be  deemed  to  have  been
cancelled.

O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
2. We had recorded in our previous orders the conduct of the
respondent, especially in orders dated 25.03.2026 and 16.04.2026
and had also issued notice in contempt.

--- Page 515 ---
2
SLP (CRL) No. 8469-8470/2025
3. We are shocked at the conduct of the respondent. When a
contempt notice has been issued and charges have been framed, the
respondent was required to appear physically before this Court on
each and every date. That not having been done itself is a ground
for strict action against him.
4. We further record that the respondent is taking chances with
the Court, inasmuch as he is failing to come up with any offer or
prayer for accommodating him for paying even a meager amount of Rs.
1,60,000/- (Rupees One Lakh Sixty Thousand), for the present,
especially when he has not been paying even for the maintenance of
his son who is specially abled.
5. Having  regard  to  the  aforesaid,  we  issue  the  following
directions.
(a) The Court below is directed to keep taking the strictest
coercive action against the respondent for such conduct.
(b) We also direct the District Magistrate of the concerned
district where the respondent resides to take action under the
relevant law and recover the amount of Rs. 1,60,000/- (Rupees one
Lakh Sixty Thousand) from the respondent, treating it as arrears of
revenue. The same be done within six weeks.
6. Let learned counsel for the petitioners serve a copy of this
order on the District Magistrate. The State of Tamil Nadu through
the District Magistrate concerned is impleaded as respondent No.2.
7. Cause title be amended accordingly.
8. The District Magistrate shall file a personally affirmed
affidavit with regard to compliance of the present order, before
the next date.

Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C)  No.30442/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  25-05-2026
in WRIC No. 10820/2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad, Lucknow Bench]
M/S ROSE BUD REALCON LLP                           Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
LUCKNOW DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY & ORS.               Respondent(s)
FOR ADMISSION 
(IA  No.  256699/2026  -  EXEMPTION  FROM  FILING  O.T.  &  IA
No.  256701/2026  -  PERMISSION  TO  FILE  ADDITIONAL
DOCUMENTS/FACTS/ANNEXURES)
 
Date : 07-09-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE J.B. PARDIWALA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) : 
                   Ms. Kamini Jaiswal, AOR
                   Ms. Rani Mishra, Adv.                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The matter is at large before the High Court.
2. The subject – matter of challenge before us is an interim
Order passed by the High Court. In the impugned Order, the High
Court has observed in Paras 7 and 8 respectively as under:-
“7. Accordingly, we do not find the details of the properties
included in the moratorium and we see no reason as to how the
Lucknow Development Authority could have rejected the application
on  this  ground.  The  impugned  order  is  therefore  illegal,
arbitrary and has been passed without any application of mind.
8. Accordingly, the Lucknow Development Authority is directed to
reconsider and file an affidavit specifically indicating as to
under which document they have concluded that the disputed
property falls under the moratoriüm under Section 14 of the Code,
2016, and it shall be open to them to pass a fresh order in

--- Page 625 ---
2
accordance with law.”
3. The learned counsel would submit that the plain reading of
Para No.7 of the impugned order, referred to above, would indicate
that the High Court has taken the final decision.
4. We are not in agreement with the submission of the learned
counsel. Para Nos.7 and 8 respectively should be read harmoniously.
5. It shall be open for the petitioner to raise all contentions
available to it in law before the High Court on the next date of
hearing.
6. With the aforesaid, the petition stands disposed of.
7. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
 (VISHAL ANAND)                                    (POOJA SHARMA)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                                 COURT MASTER (NSH)

would appear before the Mediator nominated by the Coordinator
of the Supreme Court Mediation Centre. Expenses for the same of
the wife will be borne by the husband as may be determined by
the Mediator.

conclusion of the proceedings.

remain stayed.
